impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 permits broad method claims for treating headache with any humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibody, where identifying qualifying antibodies within the claimed genus requires undue experimentation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method-of-treatment patent claims against Eli Lilly's enablement challenge. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel decision undermines enablement standards for method claims by sustaining overly broad claims contrary to Supreme Court precedent. The case has major implications for the scope of biologic and pharmaceutical patent claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the pharmaceutical and biologics space benefit from the panel ruling's more permissive enablement standard for method claims, potentially sustaining broader patent protection for therapeutic antibody inventions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor pharmaceutical and biotech companies face broader blocking patents on methods of treatment, potentially limiting freedom to operate and increasing licensing costs. The dissent signals continued uncertainty about enablement standards for genus claims.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive patent license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' to the licensee such that the licensee could sue for infringement in its own name without joining the patent owner, and whether shifting business operations to patent enforcement constituted ceasing business operations triggering license termination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, granting standing to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that shifting to enforcement-only operations did not constitute ceasing business operations under the license agreement. This clarifies when exclusive licensees can independently enforce patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive patent licensees, including patent assertion entities, benefit from clearer standards confirming their right to independently enforce patents without joining the patent owner, and that pivoting to enforcement does not terminate their license.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense based on standing defects and face continued litigation by entities whose sole business is patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding the plaintiff's trade secret damages expert and in reducing the jury's breach of contract damages award, and whether sufficient evidence supported trade secret misappropriation liability.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating it, and affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation. This case provides significant guidance on trade secret damages methodology and expert testimony standards in complex software licensing disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from the court's instruction to consider broader damages models and from the reinstatement of a full jury award on breach of contract, strengthening recovery prospects in technology licensing disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop software based on licensed technology face heightened exposure for trade secret misappropriation claims and potentially larger damages awards.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) range are indefinite under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) when the specification identifies multiple measurement methods that yield materially different results.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that claims of the '287 patent directed to waterproof breathable membranes are invalid as indefinite because the patent's MVTR limitation could be measured using different methods yielding different results, and the specification failed to provide adequate guidance on which method to use. This decision reinforces that claims with quantitative limitations must clearly specify how to measure the claimed parameter.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the materials and textiles industry can challenge patents with ambiguous measurement standards, reducing exposure to overbroad patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims reciting quantitative performance metrics face increased invalidity risk if their specifications reference multiple measurement protocols without specifying which one defines the claim scope.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for certain asserted patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement, and affirmed the damages award against LG. The split outcome on eligibility across related patents in the same case provides important guidance on how courts should analyze § 101 for claims involving digital signal processing improvements incorporated into industry standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting standard-essential patents in communications technology retain viable claims where the patents are directed to concrete technical improvements, and the damages affirmance supports robust royalty recovery.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing communications standards face continued infringement exposure and damages liability, while the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about which claim formulations survive § 101 scrutiny.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to a communications apparatus using a transformer with a non-magnetic core to match impedance for wireless signal transmission are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even though the district court found them indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness finding but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on the alternative ground of lack of enablement. The court held that the patent's claims, which purported to cover transmitting signals over air using a transformer with a non-magnetic core, were not enabled because the specification did not teach how to achieve the claimed functionality across the full scope of the claims. This demonstrates the Federal Circuit's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not reached below, providing additional defensive options in patent litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that appellate courts may invalidate their patents on grounds not fully litigated at trial, increasing unpredictability in patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the term 'internal diameter' in a patent claim directed to a float tool for oil and gas wellbore operations, and whether the resulting infringement and invalidity findings were correct.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's judgment on infringement and invalidity of a patent covering oil and gas wellbore tools, finding error in the claim construction of 'internal diameter.' The case has significant implications for patent disputes in the energy services industry, where claim construction of mechanical terms can determine infringement outcomes for widely used oilfield equipment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the energy services sector benefit from the Federal Circuit's careful scrutiny of claim construction, potentially broadening the scope of their claims on remand.
impacts.negativeImplications: Oilfield equipment manufacturers face renewed infringement risk following remand and must reassess product designs against potentially broader claim constructions.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salt satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) in a Hatch-Waxman ANDA litigation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of three Exelixis patents covering crystalline forms of the cancer drug cabozantinib have adequate written description. This ruling protects Exelixis's patent portfolio covering Cabometyx® against generic entry, with the patents not expiring until 2030. The decision reinforces the strength of pharmaceutical polymorph patents where the specification adequately discloses the claimed crystalline forms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of written description for polymorph and salt form patents, reinforcing patent protection strategies that extend exclusivity periods for blockbuster drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face delayed market entry for cabozantinib products, and the ruling may encourage broader polymorph patenting strategies that extend pharmaceutical exclusivity.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying a defendant's motion for attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and Rule 11 sanctions where the patent holder's claims were invalidated under § 101 and related patent applications had been rejected on the same grounds.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and attorneys' fees, finding that the court's order lacked sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that filed suit despite PTO rejections of related applications under § 101 and a prior court invalidation of a related patent. This signals closer scrutiny of fee-shifting decisions in patent cases involving potentially abusive enforcement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases benefit from heightened appellate scrutiny of fee-shifting denials, potentially deterring patent assertion entities from filing suits on patents with known eligibility vulnerabilities.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk of fee-shifting and sanctions when asserting patents where related claims have been rejected or invalidated under § 101.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a contract interpretation dispute arising from a patent litigation settlement agreement concerning the meaning of 'survives the EPR' in an ex parte reexamination context.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute about whether a contingent payment was owed under a patent settlement agreement, because the case turned on state-law contract interpretation rather than a substantial patent law question. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for disputes arising from patent settlement agreements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlements benefit from clarity that contractual disputes over settlement terms will be resolved in the regional circuit under state contract law, potentially providing more predictable interpretive frameworks.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties who assumed Federal Circuit jurisdiction for settlement disputes face procedural delays and venue uncertainty, and must draft settlement agreements with awareness that regional circuits will interpret ambiguous patent-related terms.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on both improper venue and patent-ineligibility grounds in the same order, rather than only dismissing for improper venue and transferring or allowing refiling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a district court's dismissal of a patent infringement case on both improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b) and patent ineligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 in a single order. The appellant did not challenge either conclusion on the merits but argued the court should not have reached eligibility after finding venue improper. The ruling confirms that district courts may address multiple grounds for dismissal simultaneously, potentially resulting in preclusive effect on eligibility determinations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain merits rulings on patent eligibility even when venue is improper, potentially creating issue preclusion that prevents refiling of invalidated claims in a proper venue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders risk losing claims on the merits when filing in an improper venue, as courts may reach eligibility determinations that foreclose future enforcement opportunities.
